description: Original Wiktionary-attributed records for the 1,704 additional 2025 baby names with sourced etymology.

abbigail.ety: A rare nonstandard spelling of Abigail.

abbygail.ety: A rare nonstandard spelling of Abigail.

abe.ety: A shortening from Abraham. In the slang sense for money, refers to the picture of Abraham Lincoln on the currency.

abrahan.ety: From American Spanish Abrahán. Doublet of Abraham and Avraham and Ibrahim and Abramo.

abubakar.m: father of a young camel; father of a person named Bakr
abubakar.ety: Borrowed from Arabic أَبُو بَكْر. This surname is predominantly found in Nigeria.

adel.ety: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aþalaz. The female name is a rare variant of Adele.

adem.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish آدم Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish آدم (adem).

adnan.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عدنان (Adnan), from Arabic عَدْنَان (“settler”).

adonai.m: sir, my lord (used when addressing a man)

adria.ety: From Latin Adria, Hadria. Compare Adriatic.

aelita.ety: From Russian Аэлита (Aelita), from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (“wind, atmosphere”).

agatha.ety: Borrowed from English Agatha, from Ancient Greek Ἀγαθή, from ἀγαθός (“good”).

agnes.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή, coming from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (“pure, chaste”), Ancient Greek ἁγνεία (“purity, chastity”). Doublet of Inez.

ahmet.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish احمد (ahmed), from Arabic أَحْمَد.

aida.ety: Borrowed from Italian Aida, made famous by Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, which premiered in 1871.

aimee.ety: Borrowed from French Aimée (“beloved”). A variation of the English Amy.

aine.ety: A derivative of Old Irish án (“bright, brilliant; splendid, noble”).

aira.ety: From airene (“ryegrass”), from Airisa as a rendering of the English Iris, or a phonetic coinage.

alanah.ety: Rare spelling variant of Alana, the feminine form of Alan.

alanis.ety: A feminine form of Alan best known for the Canadian singer Alanis Morissette whose father was named Alan.

alastair.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Alasdair (“Alexander”). Doublet of Alexander.

alberta.ety: From Albert + -a. The province was named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta.

albin.ety: Early saints' name, from the Roman cognomen Albīnus, derivative of Latin albus (“white”). In the case of individuals from Germanic nations, partly also from Germanic (cf.

albina.ety: From Latin Albina (name of a third-century martyr), feminine form of the Roman cognomen Albīnus, derivative of Latin albus (“white”).

aleks.ety: Short form of Aleksander and Alexius. Cognate with English Alex.

aleksandar.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Алеѯандръ, from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓λέξᾰνδρος. Older variant without "fleeting a": Александр.

alesha.ety: One of the modern variations of Alicia.

alexandre.ety: Borrowed from French Alexandre and Portuguese Alexandre.

alexandros.ety: Transliteration of Greek Αλέξανδρος, a male given name used in (modern) Greece. Cognate with English Alexander.

alexandru.ety: From Spanish Alejandro from Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος. Compare Xandru.

alissa.ety: Variant of Alyssa, from Alicia or from alyssum.

alister.ety: From Old Irish Alaxander, from Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος, from ἀλέξω (“to defend”) + ἀνήρ (“man”).

alon.ety: Four main origins: Borrowed from Macedonian Alen; Borrowed from English Alan.

aloysius.ety: Latinization of Occitan Aloys, an Occitan form of Louis. Doublet of Louis.

alton.ety: From Old English ǣwell (“river source”) + tūn (“settlement, town”).

alycia.ety: A rare spelling variant of Alicia.

amadeo.ety: From Amadeo. From Latin Amadeus, from Latin amo (“love”) + deus (“god”).

amadeus.ety: From Latin Amadeus, from Latin amo (“love”) + deus (“god”).

amadou.ety: A French spelling of a name ultimately derived from Arabic أَحْمَدُ, i.e. Native spellings include Wolof and Pulaar Aamadu etc.

amal.ety: From Russian Амаль (Amalʹ), from Arabic أَمَل (“hope”).

america.ety: New Latin America, feminine Latinized form of the Italian first name of Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512).

anabella.ety: Rare spelling variant of Annabella, the Latinate form of Annabel.

anastasia.ety: From Greek Αναστασία (Anastasía), from Ancient Greek ἀνάστασις (“resurrection”).

anastasija.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἀναστασία. Cognate with English Anastasia.

andra.ety: A modern feminine form of Andres (“Andrew”).

andreina.ety: Feminine (diminutive) form of Andrea (“Andrew”), comparable to the English female name Andrea.

andria.ety: Borrowed from the Ancient Greek Ανδρεία.

andriy.ety: From Ukrainian Андрі́й (“Andrew”). Doublet of Andrew.

angeles.ety: From ángeles (“angels”), shortened from María (de los) Ángeles, a Roman Catholic epithet of the Virgin Mary as the Queen of Angels.

angeline.ety: Borrowed from French Angeline, from female>.

angelino.ety: From Angelo, from diminutive suffix> From Angelo (“a male given name”) + -ino.

anh.ety: As for the country name, contracted from Chinese 英國 (Anh quốc, “United Kingdom”), from Chinese 英 (Anh) (as in Mandarin 英吉利 (Yīngjílì, Anh Cát Lợi, “England”) or 英格蘭 (Yīnggélán, Anh Cách Lan, “England”)) + 國 (quốc, “country”).

anibal.ety: Borrowed from Latin Hannibal, Annibal, from Punic 𐤇𐤍𐤁𐤏𐤋.

anina.ety: Of unknown origin. Store norske leksikon describes Anina as possibly derived from one of the female given names Anna, Anne or Ane.

anita.ety: From Spanish Anita, diminutive of Ana (“Ann”).

annette.ety: From French Annette, diminutive of Anne, from Ἄννα, the Ancient Greek New Testament form of the Hebrew female name חַנָּה (ḥannâ, “grace, gracious”) with the French suffix 'ette meaning cute, adorable or little.

anni.ety: Borrowed from English Annie (“female given name”), adapted in spelling. English Annie is a pet form of Ann and Anne.

anniston.ety: The city in Alabama, originally Woodstock, was renamed by town officials in 1873 (after realizing there was another village named Woodstock in central Alabama) in honor of Annie Eliza Scott Tyler (1838–1914).

anny.ety: Borrowed from English Anny (“female given name”), a dated spelling variant of Annie, originally a pet form of Ann and Anne.

aras.ety: From Turkish Aras, from Persian ارس (aras), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *Raxsā- (“swift-flowing”). Compare Sanskrit रङ्घते (“to hasten, run”).

arch.m: pure, holy, genuine, precious + strong, bold

archibald.m: pure, holy, genuine, precious + strong, bold
archibald.ety: From Anglo-Norman Arcebald, Arcenbald or Ercenbald, from Old French Archaunbault, from Proto-West Germanic *Erknabalþ, from *erkn (“pure, holy, genuine, precious”) + *balþ (“strong, bold”).

areg.ety: From Armenian Արեգ (Areg), from Old Armenian արեգ (“sun”).

arev.ety: From Armenian Արև (Arew), from Old Armenian արև (“sun”).

ariane.ety: From French Ariane, from Ancient Greek Ἀριάδνη.

arif.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عارف (arif), from Arabic عَارِف (“knowing”), active participle of عَرَفَ (“to know”).

arik.ety: Transcription of a modern Hebrew diminutive of the Hebrew equivalent of Ariel.

arina.ety: From Russian Арина, a variant of Ири́на (“Irene”).

arizona.ety: From O'odham alĭ ṣonak, from Basque haritz ona.

arnav.ety: From Sanskrit अर्णव (“ocean, sea”). Doublet of Arnab.

arnold.ety: From a French version of a Germanic name, from Proto-West Germanic *Arnuwald, from Proto-Germanic *arô (“eagle”) + *waldą (“power”).

arnulfo.ety: From German Arnulf derived from Germanic elements German arn (“eagle”) and German ulf (“wolf”).

arsenio.ety: From Ancient Greek Ἀρσένιος, from ἄρσην (“masculine, virile”).

arvid.ety: From Old Norse Arnviðr, arn / ǫrn (“eagle”) + viðr (“tree, wood”).

arye.ety: From Yiddish אריה (arih), from Hebrew אַרְיֵה (“lion”).

ashby.ety: From Old English æsċ (“ashtree”) + Old Norse býr (“farm, town”).

asif.ety: From Hebrew אסף (asef, “to gather”); or Persian, Urdu آصف (āsaf, “name of Solomon's vizier”).

asiya.ety: From Bengali আসিয়া (aśiẏa), from Arabic آسٍ (“healer”).

asta.ety: Old Norse Ásta, a medieval diminutive of Ástríðr (hence Astrid).

athanasia.ety: From Greek Αθανασία (Athanasía), from Ancient Greek ἀθανασία (“undying, immortal”).

athanasios.m: a-, un-, non- + dying + -y: forming adjectives
athanasios.ety: From Greek Αθανάσιος and Ancient Greek Ἀθανάσιος, from α- (“a-, un-, non-”) + θάνατος (“dying”) + -ιος (“-y: forming adjectives”). Doublet of Athanasius and Afanasy.

augusta.ety: From Latin Augusta From Latin Augusta, feminine of Augustus. The places are mostly named for British royalty.

augusto.ety: Inherited from Latin Augustus Inherited from Latin Augustus.

aurea.ety: From the feminine form of the Latin adjective aureus (“golden”).

avigail.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew אֲבִיגַיִל (avigáyil, “Avigail”), literally “my Father's joy” or “fountain of joy”.

avril.m: of the month of the goddess Venus

azalia.m: A plant of the obsolete genus Azalea.
azalia.ety: From azalia, an archaic form of azalea.

baltazar.ety: From Akkadian 𒁹𒀭𒂗𒈗𒋀 (“Bēl-šarra-uṣur”), literally “May Bel protect the king”. Cognate with English Balthazar.

bambi.ety: Borrowed from Italian Bambi, from bambina (“young girl”).

baron.m: The male ruler of a barony.

barry.ety: Anglicized form of Irish Bairre, short form of Fionnbharr, from fionn (“white”) + barr (“head”).

barton.ety: From Old English bere (“barley”) + Old English tūn (“enclosure”).

basil.ety: Name of several early saints, particularly in the Orthodox Church, from Latin Basilius, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος. Doublet of Vasilios and Vasily.

basilio.ety: From Spanish Basilio, from Latin Basilius, from Ancient Greek Βασίλειος.

baxter.ety: From Middle English bakster, bakestre, from Old English bæcestre (“baker”), equivalent to bake + -ster.

belinda.ety: From Belle + -inda, base from various Romance sources such as French belle, Italian bella (“beautiful”), suffix Latinate form of German linde (“soft”) (English linden, lithe).

benjamim.m: son of the right/south or son of days

benji.m: son of the right/south or son of days

bennet.ety: See French Benoît, Norman Beneît. Doublet of Benoit and Benito.

bennie.m: son of the right/south or son of days

benoit.ety: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin Benedictus, from benedictus (“blessed; well spoken of”), from Latin benedicō.

bento.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Bẽeito, from Late Latin Benedictus, from benedictus (“blessed”), from Latin benedicō. Doublet of Benedito and bendito.

berenice.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Βερενῑ́κη (“bringer of victory”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Macedonian (compare the native word Φερενῑ́κη), from φέρω (“to bear, to carry, to bring”) + νῑ́κη (“victory”).

berkeley.ety: From Old English beorc (“birch”) + leah (“meadow, leigh”). Equivalent to birch + -ley (“lea”).

bernie.ety: From Bernard + -ie. From Bernadette + -ie or Bernice + -ie.

bertha.ety: Definitely from Old English Berþa as a result of metathesis of h, from earlier Old English Berhte (“bright one”), influence of Latin Bercta.

beryl.ety: From beryl or an anglicization of Yiddish בערל, literally “little bear”.

betsy.ety: From the Short form of Elizabeth + -sy.

beulah.ety: A biblical name applied to the land of Israel in Isaiah 62:4, from Biblical Hebrew בְּעוּלָה (bəʿûlâ, “married (woman)”), taken up as a given name by Puritans and used figuratively for the New Earth.

beverley.ety: From Old English befer (“beaver”) + lēah (“clearing”). Equivalent to Beaver + -ley (“lea”).

bianka.ety: Borrowed from German Bianka Borrowed from German Bianka.

bill.ety: Hypocorism of William. It is unclear how the initial W became a B; this could have been part of the medieval trend of swapping letters, similar to Dick for Rick.

blanche.ety: From Old French blanc (“white”). The surname originated as a nickname, or as a matronymic.

blythe.ety: English surname, from Old English blīþe (“merry”). Many senses are derived from placenames, such as the River Blythe, all from the Old English adjective.

boyd.ety: From Scottish Gaelic, either buidhe (“blond, yellow, fair”), or a habitational surname from the Isle of Bute in Scotland.

bradford.ety: Various place names in England, from Old English brād (“broad”) + ford (“ford”).

brandt.ety: Contraction of given names containing the Germanic element *Brand-, -brand (“fire/ sword”) such as modern German Hildebrandt.

brendon.ety: Transliteration of Brandon. From Middle English Brandon, Brampdon, Bramdun, Bremedon, Bromdun, from, from brōm (“broom shrub”) + dūn (“hill, dune”).

brogan.ety: Anglicized form of Irish Ó Brógáin (“descendants of Brógán”), probably from a diminutive of bróg (“shoe”).

brook.ety: As an English surname, from the noun brook. As a north German surname, from Low German Brook (“swamp, marsh”), related to the above.

bryn.ety: From Welsh bryn (“hill, mound”), or Cumbric *brınn (“hill”) in the Greater Manchester place-name.

buck.ety: For both the English surname and given name, originally a nickname for someone who resembled a buck. Also as an English topographic surname, from Middle English buk (modern beech).

burton.ety: Usually from Old English burhtun (fortified farmstead, farmstead near or belonging to a stronghold or manor), from burh + tun.

caetano.ety: Latin Caiētānus (“inhabitant of Gaeta”), re-Latinized from Italian Gaetano, name of a saint. Compare Sicilian Caitanu.

caio.ety: From Latin Caius, variant of Gaius.

calista.ety: From Latin Callistus, from Ancient Greek Κάλλιστος (“most beautiful”), from καλός (“beautiful”). Compare Callisto.

calixto.ety: From Old Spanish Calixto, via Latin Callixtus, ultimately from Ancient Greek Κάλλιστος (“most beautiful”), from καλός (“beautiful”). Compare Calisto.

callista.ety: Borrowed from Italian Callista, a conflation from two sources, both from Ancient Greek: From Ancient Greek καλλίστη, feminine of κάλλιστος, superlative of καλός.

candice.ety: A variant of Candace associated with Late Latin candida (“whiteness”) via.

carey.ety: As a German surname, Americanized from Gehrig, Gehring. As a Welsh surname, variant of Carew.

carina.ety: A spelling variant of Karina, a newer form of Katrina, ultimately from Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη (Aikaterínē, “female given name”).

carleigh.ety: A rare spelling variant of Carly.

carol.m: A round dance accompanied by singing.
carol.ety: Shortened from Caroline. Associated by folk etymology with the English noun carol.

carole.m: A round dance accompanied by singing.

carsten.ety: From a Middle Low German variant of Christian.

casimir.ety: From a Polish royal name and saint's name Kazimierz, of Slavic origin, meaning "proclamation of peace".

caspar.ety: An older spelling variant of Kaspar and Kasper, continuing Medieval Latin Caspar.

cass.ety: As an English surname, from a pet form of Cassandra. As an Irish surname, from Ó Cais (“descendant of the curly-haired one”), from cas (“curly”).

cassie.ety: From Cass + -ie. A of Cassandra or Cassidy.

cecil.ety: From Latin Caecilius, a Roman family name derived from caecus (“blind”). The surname has absorbed the Old Welsh Seisyllt, from Latin Sextilius, from Sextus.

cecile.ety: From French Cécile, from Anglo-Norman Cecile, from Latin Caecilia.

celena.ety: Derived from Selene, the Greek goddess of the moon.

celso.ety: From Latin Celsus, from celsus (“high; elevated; noble”). Compare Sicilian Lu Ceusu.

chantal.ety: Borrowed from French Chantal in the 1960s, from the surname of a French saint Jeanne de Chantal, actually a Baroness of Chantal, a place name in France from Old Occitan cantal (“stone, moellon, rubblestone”).

charisma.m: A gift or power of leadership or authority.
charisma.ety: From the common noun charisma, from Ancient Greek χάρισμα.

charity.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.
charity.ety: From charity in the Biblical sense of Christian love; first used by Puritans. In early Christian tradition, Faith, Hope and Charity were the martyred daughters of Saint Sophia.

cheryl.ety: Coined in the early 20th century, possibly a blend of Cherie or Cherry and Beryl. (See cher for the etymology of Cherie.).

chesney.ety: From Norman place names meaning “oak grove” (cognate to French chênaie), from Picard quesne, from Vulgar Latin *cassanus, probably from Gaulish kassanos (“oak”).

chester.m: a town or city, especially a Roman one
chester.ety: From Middle English Chestre, from Old English Ċeaster, from ċeaster (“a town or city, especially a Roman one”).

chet.m: a town or city, especially a Roman one

christ.ety: Inherited from Middle High German Krist From Middle High German and Old High German Krist, from Latin Christus, from Ancient Greek Χριστός, a calque of Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšīaḥ.

christa.ety: Contraction of Christina and Christiana. Rare until the second half of the 20th century, reinforced by the German Christa.

christiana.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.
christiana.ety: From Latin Chrīstiāna; a medieval literate form of the female name Christian. Christian + -a.

christiano.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

ciaran.ety: From Old Irish Cíarán, originally a byname from ciar (“black”) + -án. Popularized by Irish saints dating back from the 5th century.

cindy.m: Cynthian (of or relating to Mount Cynthus)
cindy.ety: Shortened from Lucinda and Cinderella. In the 20th century adopted as a pet form of Cynthia.

ciro.ety: From Latin Cyrus, from Ancient Greek Κῦρος, from Old Persian 𐎤𐎢𐎽𐎢𐏁.

clair.ety: A less common spelling of Claire.

clarice.ety: Borrowed from French Clarisse, from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa (“Poor Clare”); see there for more. Doublet of Clarissa and Clarisse.

clarisse.ety: Borrowed from French Clarisse, from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa (“Poor Clare”); see there for more. Doublet of Clarissa and Clarice.

clarke.ety: From Clark, from Old English clerc (“cleric, clerk”).

claude.ety: In use from the 16th century. Borrowed from French Claude, from Latin Claudius, the name of a Roman gens.

clemence.ety: From clemence, from Latin clēmentia (“mercy; mildness”).

cleopatra.ety: From Middle English Cleopatra, from Latin Cleopatra, from Ancient Greek Κλεοπάτρα, meaning "glory of her father", from κλέος (“glory”) + πατήρ (“father”).

cletus.ety: Borrowed from Latin Clētus, short form of the papal name Anaclētus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάκλητος (“invoked”).

cliff.m: A vertical (or nearly vertical) rock face.
cliff.ety: The given name is from shortenings of the diminutives. The surname is from the noun cliff.

clifford.ety: From Old English clif (“cliff”) + ford (“ford”), a dweller at the ford by the steep bank.

clifton.ety: Literally meaning "town by a cliff." From Old English clif (“cliff”) + tūn (“town”). Analyzable as cliff + -ton.

clinton.ety: A habitational surname, derived from places named Glinton ("town on a hill") or Glympton ("settlement on the River Glyme"), from Old English + tun (“enclosure, homestead, town”), equivalent to the modern -ton.

clovis.ety: Borrowed from French Clovis, from Frankish *Hlōdowig, the same Germanic source as French Louis, Dutch Lodewijk and German Ludwig, see there for further information. Doublet of Louis and Ludwig.

coco.ety: From the Italian Coco, a surname derived from Sicilian cocu (“cook”).

colleen.ety: From the word colleen, from Irish cailín (“girl”), not used as a name in Ireland.

conan.ety: From Irish Conán, from Middle Irish Conán, from Primitive Irish ᚉᚑᚅᚐᚅᚅ, a derivative of Proto-Celtic *kū (“dog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ.

conley.ety: Anglicization of Irish Ó Conghalaigh and Ó Conghaile, patronyms of Conghalach. Doublet of Connolly.

constance.ety: From Latin Cōnstantia Doublet of Constantia.

constantin.ety: From French and Romanian Constantin, from Latin Cōnstantīnus, q.v. Doublet of Constantine and Konstadinos and Kostas and Costas.

constantine.ety: From Latin Cōnstantīnus From Latin Cōnstantīnus, from Constans and Constantius + -inus (“-ine: forming adjectives and patronymics”), from Latin cōnstāns (“constant, steadfast”) with and without -ius (“-y: forming adjectives”).

coralie.ety: Coined in France in the end of the 18th century, from Latin corallium (“coral”).

corinna.ety: From Ancient Greek, probably from κόρη (“girl, maid, daughter”); compare kore.

corrie.ety: From Scottish Gaelic coire (“cauldron, boiler; corrie”), which denotes a bowl-shaped geographical feature similar to a cirque.

cosmo.ety: Borrowed by Scotland from Italy in the 18th century.

courtney.ety: Variant of Courtenay, an aristocratic Norman surname derived from place names in Normandy, from Latin Curtenus, a personal name from curtus (“short”).

cris.ety: Short form of Christopher, Christian, Christine, and their variants.

crispin.ety: From Latin Crispinus, derivative of the Roman family name Crispus (“curly”).

cyril.ety: Via Late Latin Cȳrillus, from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος, from κύριος (“lord, master”).

daiana.ety: From the pronunciation of English Diana.

dalila.ety: From Kazakh Дәлила (Däliyla), from Arabic دَلِيل (“sign, indication, proof”).

dannie.ety: From Daniel or Daniella; from Hebrew דן, and archaic English -ie.

dany.ety: Short form of Daniel and Danielle.

darby.ety: From the English place name Derby, from Old Norse djúr (“deer”) + býr (“settlement”).

dari.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Dārius Latin Dārius.

daria.ety: Feminine form of Darius, of Old Persian origin. Name of an early Christian saint.

darleen.m: : a person who is very dear to one.

darling.m: : a person who is very dear to one.

darnell.ety: English surname, from the noun darnel (“type of ryegrass”). Also a variant of Darnall.

dawn.m: To begin to brighten with daylight.

daya.ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit दया (“pity, mercy, compassion”).

deirdre.ety: From Irish Deirdre, from Old Irish Derdriu.

delmar.ety: Contraction of Delamare and de la Mare, from places in Normandy named La Mare (“the pond”). In the US, also borrowed from Catalan del Mar (“of the sea”).

demetria.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess

demetrio.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess
demetrio.ety: Borrowed from Latin Demetrius, from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος.

demetrios.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess
demetrios.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος.

denton.ety: From Old English denu (“valley, den”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

diane.ety: An anglicization of French Diane, from Latin Diāna. Doublet of Diana.

didier.ety: Inherited from Latin Desiderius, from desiderium (“desire, longing”).

dietrich.ety: Inherited from Middle High German Dietrich, from Old High German Diotrih, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Þeudōrīks.

dima.m: belonging to Δημήτηρ, the earth goddess
dima.ety: From Russian Ди́ма, a diminutive of the male given name Дми́трий (“Demetrius”).

dimitry.ety: From Russian Дмитрий from Ancient Greek Δημήτριος.

dina.ety: Equivalent of the biblical name Dinah in several European languages, ultimately from Hebrew דִּינָה.

diogo.ety: The Portuguese equivalent of Spanish Diego, from Old Galician-Portuguese Diago, from Latin Didacus.

dionne.ety: From French Dionne From Latin Dione, from Ancient Greek Διώνη.

dirk.ety: Borrowed from Dutch and North German Dirk.

dmitry.ety: From Russian Дми́трий, from Medieval Greek Δημήτριος, from Δημήτηρ (“Demeter”) + -ιος (“pertaining to”). Doublet of Demetrius and Dimitri and Dimitris.

donna.ety: A 19th-century invention from the Italian noun donna; also interpreted as a feminine form of Donald.

dora.ety: A diminutive of Dorothy used since early 19th century. Sometimes also short for Theodora or Isidora.

dorcas.ety: From Ancient Greek Δορκάς (“gazelle”), translation of Tabitha in the Bible.

doris.ety: From Ancient Greek Δωρίς. is owing to similarity to Boris.

duane.ety: Anglicized form of the Irish name Dubhán (from Primitive Irish ᚇᚑᚃᚐᚌᚅᚔ), from dubh (“black, dark”); or transferred from the surname, which is from Irish Ó Dubháin, literally “descendant of Dubhán”.

dulcie.ety: From Latin dulcis (“sweet”) in the 19th century, probably inspired by earlier names like Dowsabel and Spanish Dulcinea.

eamon.ety: Borrowed from Irish Éamann (“Edmund”). Doublet of Edmund.

ean.ety: From Manx Ean, an equivalent of John.

eben.ety: Shortened from Ebenezer; equivalent to Hebrew אֶבֶן (éven, “stone”).

ebenezer.ety: From Hebrew אֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר (éven ha`ézer, “stone of help”).

eda.ety: From Old English ead (“riches”), also short for compound given names beginning thus, particularly Edith.

edmund.ety: From Old English Ēadmund, from ēad (“prosperity”) + mund (“protection”). Doublet of Eamon.

edna.ety: From Hebrew עֶדְנָה (“pleasure; delight”); a variant of Eden in the Book of Tobit.

edric.ety: From Old English Ēadrīc, from Proto-West Germanic *Audarīk, from Proto-Germanic *Audarīks, from *audaz (“wealth, riches”) + *rīks (“king, ruler”).

edrick.ety: From Old English Ēadrīc, from Proto-Germanic *Audarīks, from *audaz (“wealth, riches”) + *rīks (“king, ruler”).

edson.ety: From Ed + -son; originally given to the son of a man named Ed.

eduard.ety: From French Édouard, doublet of Edward.

edwina.ety: Female form of Edwin from Old English, equivalent to Edwin + -a.

edy.ety: From Middle English Udy, Ude, Latinized as Udo and Odo.

effie.ety: From Euphemia + -ie, or, very rarely, from modern Greek Eftychia or Euthemia (diminutive form).

einar.ety: From Old Norse Einarr, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”) and *harjaz (“warrior”). Doublet of einherje.

eira.ety: From an Old Norse goddess of medicine, Eir, eir (“relief”).

eirik.ety: Inherited from Old Norse Eiríkr (“male given name”), from Proto-Norse *Aina-rīkijaʀ (“sole ruler”) or *Aiwa-rīkijaʀ (“everlasting ruler”).

elbert.ety: A cognate of the more common Albert.

eliane.m: of pertaining to the gens Aelia.
eliane.ety: From Latin Aeliana, feminine derivative of the plebeian gens name Aelius.

elie.ety: Variously a form of Elijah used in Romanian, French, and some other languages, or short for names like Eliezer.

elin.ety: Medieval variant of Helene (Helen), comparable to English Ellen.

elis.ety: Short form of Eliisabet or Elisabeth.

elli.ety: Diminutive of Elina (“Helen”), later also Eleonoora (“Eleanor”) and likely of Elisabet.

ellinor.ety: A rare spelling variant of Elinor or Eleanor.

elma.ety: A 19th-century creation, usually explained as a form of Wilhelmina or Italian Guglielma. It has also been recorded as a blend of Elizabeth and Mary.

eloi.m: to pick, to choose from + -y: forming adjectives and names
eloi.ety: From French Éloi, from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere (“to pick, to choose from”) + -ius (“-y: forming adjectives and names”).

elroy.ety: Derived from Leroy, but with the le in "Leroy" being replaced with its corresponding equivalent in Spanish el.

elsi.ety: From English Elsie, though it may be also be a Finnish diminutive form of Elsa.

elton.ety: From a number of sources, including: # For the places in Cheshire, County Durham, and Derbyshire, England: from Old English ēl (“eel”) + tūn (“farm, village”) since the village is situated above a small stream.

elvira.ety: A medieval Spanish royal name, of probably Gothic origin, and debated meaning, possibly 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐌻𐌾𐌰𐌽 + *𐍅𐌴𐍂𐌴𐌹, thus "joyful sincerity".

elwood.ety: From the Middle English personal name Elwald, Elwold, Alwold, which is composed of the Old English elements ælf (“elf”) and weald (“rule”).

emeric.ety: Taken from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home”) + *rīkiją (“ruler”); cf. *Haimarīks. Cognate to French Henri and English Emery or Henry.

emile.m: striving to equal or excel, rivaling

emili.m: striving to equal or excel, rivaling

emilie.ety: A Norwegian variant of Emilia, ultimately from Latin Aemilia (“female given name”), the feminine form of the Roman nomen Aemilius.

emmi.ety: Originally a diminutive of Emilia and Emma.

emre.ety: From Old Turkic (amran-, “to love, desire”). Also related to Old Turkic (amrıl-, “to be quiet”), (amul, “gentle, quiet”), derived from Proto-Turkic *ăm-.

emrys.ety: From Proto-Brythonic *Ėmrös, from Latin Ambrosius, from Ancient Greek ἀμβρόσιος (“immortal, divine”).

enid.ety: From Middle Welsh eneit (“spirit, life; purity”), from Proto-Celtic *anatyom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”).

enola.ety: Created for the titular character in the 1886 American novel Enola, derived from alone spelled backwards.

enver.ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish انور (Enver), from Arabic أَنْوَر.

enza.ety: From Enzo + -a, ultimately of Germanic origin.

erasmo.ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Erasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐράσμιος (“pleasant”); name of an early Christian martyr.

eris.ety: From erë (“wind”), probably contaminated with Ancient Greek ἔρις (“strife”).

erling.ety: Old Norse Erlingr, related to jarl, "son or descendant of an earl".

erwin.ety: From Old High German heri (“army”) + wini (“friend”). Taken to regular use from the play Erwin und Elmire (1775) by Goethe.

esa.ety: Medieval vernacular form of Esaias, the old biblical equivalent of English Isaiah. It has also been recorded as a diminutive of Esko and Esau.

esmee.ety: Anglicized spelling of the French Esmée or Esmé.

estefania.ety: From Spanish Estefanía with a stress shift. Alternatively from Portuguese Estefânia, which is stressed as in German, but is nevertheless a less likely origin.

ethel.ety: Short form of names of Old English origin beginning with Ethel-, æþele (“noble”). First used in the 19th century.

etienne.ety: Inherited from Old French Estiene, from earlier Estiefne, from Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek Στέφανος. Doublet of Stéphane, a borrowing from Latin.

eugenie.m: good, well + born a certain way

evert.ety: From a diminutive of Dutch Everard or Everhard, equivalent to English Everett.

everton.ety: From Old English eofor (“wild boar”) + tūn (“settlement”).

evita.ety: From Spanish Evita, a pet form of Eva.

ewan.ety: From Scottish Gaelic Eòghan. Not related to Iwan and Evan.

ezio.ety: From Ancient Greek ᾱ̓ετός (“eagle”), either through the Latin given name Aetius or directly from Ancient Greek.

fabrice.m: skillful, one who works with hands
fabrice.ety: Borrowed from Latin Fabricius, name of a plebeian Roman gens, of unknown origin, but often explained as from faber (“skillful, one who works with hands”).

faustino.ety: From the Roman cognomen Latin Faustinus, diminutive of faustus (“favorable”).

felicia.ety: From Middle English Felicia, from Latin Fēlīcia, from fēlīcia, literally “happy things”, the neuter plural of fēlīx, which often occurred in the phrase tempora fēlīcia (“happy times”).

feliciana.ety: Latin Fēlīciāna, feminine of Fēlīciānus. Felicia + -ana or Felician + -a.

ferris.ety: English surname, from Norman Ferrers, from the toponymic Ferrières, from French fer (“iron”).

fiadh.ety: From fiadh, pre-reform spelling of fia, from Old Irish fíad (“wild; game, deer”).

filip.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος.

finlay.ety: Anglicized from Scottish Gaelic Fionnlagh (“fair warrior/hero”).

finnian.ety: From Irish, variant of Fionnán; see fionn (“fair”).

fleur.ety: French fleur (“flower”), name of a character in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga.

florentina.ety: Borrowed from Late Latin Flōrentīna, name of a Visigothic saint (died c. 612 AD); also the feminine equivalent of Latin Flōrentīnus, literally “Florentine, from Florence”.

floyd.ety: Anglicisation of the Welsh name Lloyd, from Welsh llwyd (“grey, grey-haired”).

francois.ety: Borrowed from French François, from Medieval Latin Franciscus.

franz.ety: From German Franz. Doublet of Francis.

freda.ety: A feminine form of Frederick and Fred, also a short form of Winifred.

frederik.ety: From Middle Dutch Vrederic, from Old Dutch Frithoric, from Proto-West Germanic *Friþurīk, from Proto-Germanic *Friþurīks, a compound of *friþuz (“peace”) + *rīks (“king”).

freeman.ety: Proprialisation of freeman. From originating as a freeman (instead of a serf, indentured, or some other status) free + man.

freja.ety: From Old Norse Freyja, from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ.

frieda.ety: From Elfriede. From Old English Ælfþrȳþ; later partly merged with æþel (“noble”) + þrȳþ (“strength”) ( =Audrey).

fritz.ety: Borrowed from German Fritz, pet form of Friedrich (“Frederick”).

galina.ety: Borrowed from Гали́на, from Ancient Greek γαλήνη (“calm”), name of a Nereid and of early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

galo.ety: Derived from Latin Gallus, from Latin gallus (“rooster”).

gareth.ety: Of Old Welsh origin and cognate with the Welsh name Geraint (from Latin Gerontius (“old man”), from Ancient Greek γέρων (“old man”)) or perhaps the word gwareddawg, gwaredd (“gentleness”); see gwâr (“gentle”).

garland.ety: English surname, from the noun garland. Also derived from Garland in Devon, from an ancestor of the noun gore (“triangular piece of land”) + land.

garrick.ety: From Old English *Gārrīċ, from Proto-Germanic *Gaizarīks. Doublet of Gaiseric.

gene.m: good, well + born a certain way

geneva.ety: Thumb|canton of Geneva (sense 2) Mentioned in Latin texts as Genava.

geoffrey.ety: From Middle English Geffrey, from an Old French aristocratic name, Geoffroi (> West, East ), itself from Proto-French forms (latinized in -us) Jotfredus, Jozsfredus, Josfredus (10th century) and Jof[f]redus, Jofridus, Jaufredus.

georgina.ety: From George + -ina, feminine form of George..

gerard.ety: From Middle English Gerard, from Old French Gerart, from Frankish *Gaiʀahard, from *gaiʀ (“spear”) + *hard(ī) (“hard, brave”).

german.ety: From Latin Germānus, Germānī (“the peoples of Germānia”), as distinct from Gauls (in the writings of Caesar and Tacitus), and of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly Celtic/Gaulish).

geronimo.ety: Inherited from Latin Hierōnymus, from Ancient Greek Ἱερώνυμος (“holy name”).

gerrit.ety: A by-form of Gerard, which derives from Middle Dutch Gherart, from Old Dutch *Gērhard, from Proto-West Germanic *Gaiʀahard.

gertrude.ety: From Old French, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz (“spear”) + *þrūþiz (“strength”) or *trut- (“maiden, dear”); name of a Belgian seventh century saint.

ghali.ety: From Kazakh Ғали (Ğalıy), from Arabic عَلِيّ (“high, exalted”).

gigi.ety: Borrowed from French Gigi. Sometimes a pet form of English names such as Virginia or Genesis.

giles.ety: Medieval English form of Old French saints' name Giles, modern Gilles, an altered form of Latin Aegīdius, from Ancient Greek Αἰγίδιος, derivative of αἰγίδιον (“kid, young goat”).

gina.ety: Short form of Georgina. Short form of Regina.

giovana.ety: Borrowed from Italian Giovanna. Doublet of Joana, which was inherited from Latin, of Doublet of Ivana and Jeane, borrowings from Russian and French, respectively.

gisella.ety: Borrowed from Italian Gisella, from French Giselle.

glenda.ety: Coined in the twentieth century from Welsh glân (“holy, fair”) and da (“good”).

glory.ety: From glory as a variant of the more common Gloria.

godfrey.ety: From Old French Godefrei, from Old High German Godafrid (“peace of God”), from Proto-Germanic *Gudafriþuz. Equivalent to god + frith.

golden.m: Made of, or relating to, gold.
golden.ety: As an English surname, from the adjective golden. As an Irish surname, from mag Ualghairg; see McGoldrick.

grecia.ety: Borrowed from Latin Graecia, from Ancient Greek Γραικός.

gunther.ety: From Old High German gund (“battle”) + heri (“army”), from Proto-Germanic *Gunþiharjaz. Name of a king in the Nibelungenlied, and of a medieval German saint.

gustav.ety: From Old Swedish Gøtstaf, from Old Norse Gautr (“Geats”) + stafr (“staff”).

gustave.ety: From French Gustave. French form of Swedish royal name Gustav; see Gustav for more.

guy.ety: From the Hebrew name גַּיְא (gáy), literally “valley”, with the spelling influenced by the existing English name.

gwendoline.m: white, fair, blessed + ring, bow, hair, brow

hakan.ety: From Persian خاقان (xâqân), a Persianized variant of Old Turkic 𐰴𐰍𐰣 (qaɣan). Cognate with Turkish Kaan, kağan.

hal.ety: A diminutive lambdacism of Harry (compare Sally from Sarah and Moll from Mary).

haleigh.ety: Variant spelling of Haley with the suffix -leigh.

halina.ety: Borrowed from Belarusian Галі́на, from Ancient Greek γαλήνη (“calm”), name of a Nereid and of early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

hamilton.ety: From Old English *Hameldūne, from hamel (“blunt, flat-topped”) + dūne (“hill”). The Scottish surname is from the place in Leicestershire.

hamish.ety: Anglicized spelling of Scottish Gaelic Sheumais, vocative case of Seumas, from English James (see for more). Doublet of James etc.

hampton.ety: Variously from: Old English Hāmtūn, from hām and tūn (equivalent to home + town); Old English hēantūn, from hēah and tūn (equivalent to high + town).

hania.ety: From Ottoman Turkish خانیه (Hanya) and irregular romanization of Greek Χανιά, q.v.

hans.ety: Borrowed from German Hans, a medieval short form of Johannes (“John”), ultimately from Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”). in Norway.

hardy.ety: As an English, Scottish, and French surname, from Middle English hardy, hardi, from Old French hardi (“hardy, daring, stout, bold”).

heinrich.ety: From Old High German Heimrih, Haimirich (8th century), composed of heim (“home”) + -rih (“suffix for male names, originally a noun meaning king”); corresponds to Proto-West Germanic *Haimarīk, from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks.

helene.ety: From French Hélène and from German Helene. Doublet of Helen and Helena and Elaine.

heloise.ety: From Medieval Latin Heloisa under influence from French Héloïse, probably from French Éloi + -se (“-ess: feminizing nouns”), from Medieval Latin Eligius, chiefly after Saint Eligius, from Latin ēligere (“to pick.

hendrik.ety: From Middle Dutch Hendric, Henric, from Old Dutch *Hēmrīk, *Heimrīk, from Proto-West Germanic *Haimarīk, from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks.

hercules.ety: From Latin Herculēs, from Etruscan 𐌇𐌄𐌓𐌂𐌋𐌄, from Ancient Greek Ἡρακλῆς, apparently cognate of Ἥρα (“Hera”) and, according to Haudry, from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”) + κλέος (“glory”).

herman.ety: From Old English here (“army”) + man (“man”) It was revived in the 19th century, partly due to American immigrants from continental Europe where the name has been more popular.

hermione.ety: From the Ancient Greek Ἑρμῐόνη. Not related to German Hermine.

hershel.ety: Borrowed from Yiddish הירשעל, a diminutive of הירש (“deer, buck”).

hilary.ety: From Latin Hilarius (“cheerful, happy”), name of a fourth-century saint, and from its feminine form Hilaria.

hilda.ety: Short form of Germanic names beginning or ending in hild (“battle”).

hildegard.ety: Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Hildigardu, from Proto-Germanic *hildiz (“battle”) + *gardaz (“enclosure”), with the approximate meaning “battle protector”.

hillary.ety: From Latin Hilarius or Hilaria, from hilare (“cheerfully”) (compare English hilarious).

holley.ety: As an English surname, spelling variant of Holly.

holli.ety: A rare spelling variant of Holly.

homero.ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ὅμηρος, from ὅμηρος (“hostage”). Compare Latin Homērus.

honor.ety: Shortened from Honoria and Honora; later also interpreted as a virtue name by Puritans.

howell.ety: From Welsh Hywel. Doublet of Huell and Powell.

hubert.ety: From Old French Hubert, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“mind”) + *berhtaz (“bright, famous”). See Saint Hubert.

iain.ety: From Scottish Gaelic. Cognate of John; see there for more.

ignatius.ety: From Latin Ignātius, variant of gens name Egnātius, altered to resemble ignis (“fire”), establishing a folk etymology meaning akin to “Fiery One”.

igor.ety: Transliterated from Russian И́горь, a Varangian name derived from Old Norse Yngvarr, Ingvarr, from Yngvi (name of a god) + herr (“army”). Doublet of Ivor and Ihar and Ihor.

ilias.ety: Borrowed from Arabic إِلْيَاس, from Ancient Greek Ἠλίας, from Hebrew אֵלִיָּהוּ (eliyáhu), whence also Elia, Elias.

ilma.ety: From in the 19th century. Also shortened from Ilmatar, ilman impi, spirits of air in Finnish mythology.

ilona.ety: From Hungarian Ilona. A rare variant of Helen or Helena.

ilya.ety: From Russian Илья́. Doublet of Elijah.

ilyas.ety: Borrowed from Arabic إِلْيَاس, from Hebrew אליהו.

imanol.ety: Coined by Sabino Arana from Hebrew עִמָּנוּאֵל ('imánuel).

imelda.ety: From Spanish Imelda, from Imelda Lambertini, from Proto-Germanic *ermunaz (“all, whole”) + *hildiz (“battle”).

imogen.ety: First used by William Shakespeare in Cymbeline, a misprint for Innogen, from Scottish Gaelic inghean (“girl, maiden”).

ina.ety: Short form of given names ending in -ina, e.g. Georgina, Christina, Wilhelmina.

indra.ety: From Sanskrit इन्द्र. Doublet of indra.

ines.ety: From Latin Agnes, from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή, from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (“pure, chaste”), Ancient Greek ἁγνεία (“purity, chastity”).

inez.ety: Anglicised form of Spanish Inés and Portuguese Inês, both from Latin Agnes, from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή. First used in 18th century English poetry and plays referring to Inês de Castro.

inga.ety: From Danish, Norwegian, Swedish Inga etc., all from Old Norse Inga.

inna.ety: Transliteration of Russian И́нна, of uncertain origin. (One suggestion is Ancient Greek ἴννα, from ἴννην (“little girl”).).

ion.ety: A non-standard spelling of Jon, the sequence io stands for.

irina.ety: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Ирина, from Ancient Greek Εἰρήνη, from εἰρήνη (“peace”).

irwin.ety: From a medieval given name Erwin, from Eoforwine, from Old English eofor (“boar”) + wine (“friend”), the latter of which is from Proto-West Germanic *wini.

isaak.ety: Borrowed from Latin Isaāc, from Ancient Greek Ἰσαᾱ́κ, from Biblical Hebrew יִצְחָק (Yiṣḥāq), literally “he laughs”.

isabell.ety: From Isabel. From Spanish Isabel, Portuguese Isabel.

isadora.ety: A variant of Isidora, from Latin Isidōra, equivalent of Īsidōrus, from Ancient Greek Ῑ̓σῐ́δωρος (“gift of Isis”).

isidora.ety: Name of a fourth-century saint. The feminine equivalent of Isidore, from Ancient Greek Ἰσιδώρα (“gift of Isis”).

isidore.ety: French form of the name of early Spanish saints, from Ancient Greek Ἰσίδωρος, meaning "gift of (the goddess) Isis".

isolde.ety: Borrowed from the German Isolde, German form of Iseult.

iva.ety: From Ivo. A hypocoristic form of Ivan.

ivar.ety: From Old Norse Ívarr, from Proto-Norse *ᛁᚹᚨᚺᚨᚱᛃᚨᛉ, from Proto-Germanic *īwaz (“yew tree, bow”) + *harjaz (“warrior, army”); also partly merged with Old Norse Yngvarr.

izzy.ety: From the root of the names + -y.

janet.ety: From Jane + -et, q.v. Chiefly Scottish until the 19th century.

jani.ety: From Swedish Jan, a diminutive of (a cognate of) Johannes.

janina.ety: From Polish Janina and possibly other Slavic languages as well.

janine.ety: From French Janine and Jeannine under influence from Jane, from Jeanne + -ine, q.v.

janna.ety: Either a feminine derivative of Jan or a contracted form of Johanna. Both source names belong to the Johannes name family.

january.ety: From Middle English Januarie, januari, re-latinised forms of Middle English Janevere, Ieneuer, from Anglo-Norman genever, from Latin Iānuārius (“(month) of Janus”), a compound of Iānus + -ārius.

jarrett.ety: Variant of Garrett, a medieval form of Gerard and Gerald.

jarvis.ety: A surname derived from a Middle English form of Gervase.

jayse.ety: Non-standard spelling of Jase or Jace.

jazz.ety: A fanciful spelling variant of Jaz and Jas.

jean.ety: From French Jean, from Old French Jehan, from Latin Iōhannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוחנן (Yôḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

jeanette.ety: From Jean + -ette or misspelling of French Jeannette, from Jeanne + -ette, q.v. Originally chiefly Scottish.

jeanne.ety: From French Jeanne, from Middle French Jehanne, from Medieval Latin Johanna, variant of Latin Ioanna under influence from Latin Iōhannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”.

jeannette.ety: From French Jeannette, from Jeanne + -ette, q.v.

jeannine.ety: From French Jeannine, from Jeanne + -ine, q.v. Sometimes also parsed as a diminutive of English Jean, Jeanne, etc.

jeff.ety: From Jeffrey, a variant of Geoffrey, from Middle English Geffrey, from an Old French aristocratic name, Geoffroi (> West, East ), itself from Proto-French forms (latinized in -us) Jotfredus, Jozsfredus.

jelena.ety: Borrowed from Еле́на and Pannonian Rusyn Єлена, from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη. Doublet of Helen and Ellen.

jemima.ety: From the name of a minor biblical character, from Hebrew יְמִימָה (“dove”). By folk etymology also used as a feminine form of James.

jenessa.ety: Most likely a Blend of Jennifer + Vanessa.

jenny.ety: From Jen + -y, historically as a hypocoristic form of Janet, Jane, etc. but now more often used as a diminutive of Jennifer.

jens.ety: Medieval vernacular form of Johannes (“John”). Recorded in Denmark since the 14th century.

jeremie.ety: From Latin Jeremias From Latin Jeremias, from Ancient Greek Ἰερεμίας, from Biblical Hebrew יִרְמְיָה (Yirməyâ, “Jeremiah”), literally “the will raise”.

jeronimo.ety: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin Hierōnymus, from Ancient Greek Ῑ̔ερώνυμος, from ἱερός (“sacred”) + ὄνομα (“name”).

jewell.ety: From Middle English - Medieval/Middle English form of a Breton saint's name, from Old Breton Judicaël "lord" + "generous." The second element is from hael (“generous.

jibril.ety: Borrowed from Arabic جِبْرِيل Doublet of Gabriel.

jill.ety: A variant of Gill, diminutive of Gillian, a medieval form of Juliana, ultimately from Latin.

jo.ety: Short form of names with the element jo (such as Jostein and Jorid), from jór (“horse”).

joachim.ety: From Latin Iōākīm, from Ancient Greek Ἰωακείμ, Ἰωακίμ (2 Kings 24:1), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹיָקִים (yəhôyâqîm), literally “may Yahweh raise up”.

joanne.ety: From Old French Joanne, from Latin Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”, the feminized form of יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān) which produced John and its many doublets.

joao.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Joan, from Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Iōannēs, from New Testament Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης, contraction from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (yôḥānān), literally “God is gracious”.

jocelynn.ety: A rare non-standard spelling of Jocelyn with -lynn.

jody.ety: Variant of Judy, diminutive of Judith, q.v.

johann.ety: Borrowed from German Johann (“male given name”), a short form of Johannes (“male given name”), ultimately from Latin Iōhannēs (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs, “male given name”).

johnna.ety: A rare feminine form of John recorded since the 18th century.

johnson.ety: A patronymic surname from John + -son, literally “son of John”.

jona.ety: From Biblical Hebrew יוֹנָה (Yōnā, “dove”), through biblical tradition. The form corresponds more closely to the Hebrew name than Jonas, whose final ⟨s⟩ reflects the Greek and Latin nominative forms.

joni.ety: Commonly used as a diminutive of Joan.

jori.ety: Phonetic rendering of Swedish Georg (“George”). Also recorded as a pet form of Jorma.

josef.ety: From Latin Iōsēphus, from Ancient Greek Ἰωσήφ, from Hebrew יוֹסֵף (“(God) shall add”). Doublet of Albanian Jozef (“Joseph”).

jozef.ety: From Latin Iōsēphus, from Ancient Greek Ἰωσήφ, from Hebrew יוֹסֵף.

juanita.ety: From Spanish Juanita, from Juana + -ita (“-ette”), from Old Spanish Johanna, from Medieval Latin Johanna, variant of Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh), literally “God is gracious”.

juanito.ety: From Juan, equivalent to the English John.

judd.ety: From a Middle English short form of the given name Jordan.

jules.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.

juli.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.
juli.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Iūlius Latin Iūlius.

juliann.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.
juliann.ety: A variant of Julian, Juliana or Julianne. Can also be interpreted as a combination of Julia + Ann.

julianne.m: Of the gens Julia, a patrician Roman family.
julianne.ety: A 19th/20th century variant of Juliana. Can also be interpreted as a combination of Julia + Anne.

juni.ety: From juni (“June”), partly as a translation of the English given name June.

justine.ety: From French Justine, from Latin Iūstīna, name of early saints, feminine of Iūstīnus, derivative of Iūstus, from iūstus (“just”). The feminine equivalent of Justin.

kaidence.m: The act or state of declining or sinking.

kaila.ety: Kaila (“style”),a loan word from English style; can also be construed as ka (“the”) + ila (“dark birthmark; darkness; seedling”).

kaili.ety: Modern combination of Kai (“Catherine”) and Lii (“Elizabeth”).

kaja.ety: 20th century creation from kaja (“echo”). Also interpreted as a variant of Kaia, from Katariina (“Catherine”).

kalena.ety: Ka (“the”) + lena (“yellow”).(Yellow was a royal color.) Later also used as a phonetic rendering of the English Karen.

karleigh.ety: A rare spelling variant of Carly.

kasandra.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Κασσάνδρα.

kaspar.ety: A variant of Kasper, reflecting the older continental European form Caspar or Kaspar.

kasper.ety: Variant of Kaspar, from Medieval Latin Caspar (“male given name”), traditionally the name of one of the Magi in Western Christianity.

katarina.ety: From the Ancient Greek Αἰκατερίνη, name of a saint.

katharine.ety: A variant spelling of Catherine, based on the folk etymology that it would derive from Greek καθαρός (katharos "pure").

katya.ety: Transliteration of Ка́тя, diminutive of Екатери́на, Катери́на.

keeley.ety: Reduced Anglicized from Irish Ó Caollaidhe (“descendant of Caollaidhe”), a personal name based on the adjective caol (“slender, graceful”).

keelin.ety: Borrowed from Irish Caoilfhionn, from caol (“thin, slender”) + fionn (“light, fair”).

kelli.ety: From Kerli. Combination of Kertu (“Gertrude”) and Lii (“Elizabeth”).

kendal.ety: From Old English Cent + dæl = "valley of the river Kent".

kenley.ety: Shortened from McKenley, variant of McKinley Habitational from Old English Cena (“a man's name”) + lēah (“woodland clearing”).

kent.ety: Inherited from Middle English Kent, from Old English Cent, from Latin Cantium, from Brythonic *Cantio (compare Old Irish céite (“gathering, folkmoot, hillock”)), from Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim”).

kenton.ety: From either the Old English personal name Cena or cyne- (“royal”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

keona.ety: Ke (“the”) + ona (“attractive”). Also a short form of compound given names beginning thus.

kerrigan.ety: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Ciaragáin (“grandson/descendant of Ciaragán”), a byname from a double diminutive of ciar (“black”).

kerry.ety: As an English surname, from a personal name derived from Old Norse Kári. As an Irish surname, from Ó Ciardha (“descendant of Ciardha”), from ciar (“black”).

kezia.ety: From Hebrew קְצִיעָה (“cassia tree”). Compare cassia.

kim.ety: Short form of Kimball and Kimberley as a male name, and of Kimberley and Kimberly as a female name.

kimberley.ety: English place name "wood or clearing of Kyneburga (a seventh century female saint)", from Old English cyne- (“royal”) + burh (“fortress”) + lēah (“leigh, clearing”).

kirby.ety: Originally Kirkby, from kirk (“church”) + -by (“habitation”), "village with a church".

kirill.ety: From Russian Кири́лл, from Ancient Greek Κύριλλος. Doublet of Cyril.

kirsten.ety: From North Germanic (Danish Kirsten and Norwegian Kirsten). Doublet of Christina.

klara.ety: Borrowed from Latin clāra, feminine of clārvs (“bright, shining, clear”), a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara (Clare) of Assisi.

konrad.ety: From Middle High German Kuonrāt, from Old High German Kuonrad, Chuonrad, from Proto-West Germanic *Kōnirād; equivalent to Proto-West Germanic *kōnī (“bold, brave”) + *rād (“counsel”).

krista.ety: A spelling variant of Christa, a modern short form of Christina, partly borrowed from German Christa.

kristel.ety: Variant of Kristiina (“Christina”). Cognate with German Christel.

kristen.ety: A spelling variant of Kristin, from Christina, fairly popular in the latter half of the twentieth century.

kristiana.ety: From Latin Christiana. Feminine form of Kristiāns (“Christian”).

kristin.ety: Borrowed in the 20th century from Norwegian Kristin, a variant of Christina.

kristina.ety: From Latin Christina (“female given name”), a feminine derivative of Christianus (“Christian; male given name”), from Latin Christus (“Christ”), from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós, “anointed”), from χρίω (khríō, “to anoint”).

kristoffer.ety: Saint's name of Ancient Greek origin, cognate with English Christopher.

krystian.m: Christian; of those who believe in Christ.

ksenia.ety: Transliteration of Ксения. Borrowed from Carpathian Rusyn Ксенія and/or Serbo-Croatian Ксенијa//Ksenija, ultimately from Ancient Greek ξενία.

kurt.ety: From kurt (“wolf”), from Ottoman Turkish قورت (Kurt).

laina.ety: Proposed as a new given name in the 19th century. Perhaps from laina (“loan”), with the philosophy that children are but a loan to their parents.

lambert.ety: From Middle English Lambert, from Old French Lambert, a saint's name (of a Bishop of Maastricht) brought to England by the Normans, from Proto-West Germanic *Landaberht, from *land (“land”) + *berht (“bright”).

lancelot.ety: From Middle English Launcelot, from Old French Lancelot, from Frankish *Lanzo, hypocoristic form of names beginning in *Land-, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), and diminutive Old French endings -el and -ot.

lars.ety: Borrowed from North Germanic, from Latin Laurentius.

laszlo.ety: Borrowed from Hungarian László, from the Slavic given name Ladislav, a variant of Vladislav. Doublet of Ladislaus.

laurence.ety: From the name of a third century Roman martyr, Latin Laurentius, "a person from Laurentum", the place name possibly derived from laurus (“laurel”).

laurent.ety: From Old French Lorenz, from Latin Laurentius.

lauretta.ety: An Italian pet form of Laura; first introduced into English as the name of one of the narrators in the Decameron.

laurie.ety: The given names are s of Short form of Laurence,Lawrence,Laura,Lauren -ie, all ultimately from Latin laurus (“laurel”).

lauro.ety: From the Italian surname, from a personal name derived from Latin laurus.

lavanya.ety: From Telugu లావణ్య (lāvaṇya), from Sanskrit लावण्य (“beauty”).

lawton.ety: From Middle English, from Old English, from hlāw (“hill, ound”) + tūn (“homestead”) (-ton).

lazar.ety: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian Lazar, ultimately from Ancient Greek Λάζαρος, from Hebrew אלעזר (ʼElʻāzār).

leeroy.ety: A less common spelling variant of Leroy.

leigh.ety: From the nominative case of Old English lēah (“wood, meadow”), 'dweller by the wood or clearing'.

lenin.ety: Borrowed from Russian Ле́нин Borrowed from Russian Ле́нин.

leonid.ety: Borrowed from Леони́д or Ukrainian Леоні́д, from Ancient Greek Λεωνίδας. Cognate with the English historical name Leonidas.

leonie.ety: From French Léonie, from Latin Leonia, feminine of Leonius, derived from leo (“lion”).

leonora.ety: From the Italian short form of Eleonora, cognate to Eleanor.

leopold.ety: From Old French Leopold, from Old High German liut (“people”) + bald (“bold”). The first part is sometimes associated by folk etymology with Latin leo (“lion”), as in Leo and Leonard.

lesley.ety: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally Lesslyn, Scottish Gaelic lios cuileann (“garden of hollies”).

levin.ety: From Russian Левин, from Леви + -ин (“forming possessives & adjectives”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (“Levi”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Levine.

lexa.ety: A short form of Alexa or Alexandra.

leyton.ety: From the name of the River Lea + Old English tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”). Doublet of Luton.

lilli.ety: Pet form of female given names containing the syllable -li-, such as Eliisabet and Aliide. Also explained as Estonian lill (“flower”).

lillyanna.ety: Variant of Liliana, or from Lily + Anna.

linden.ety: As a Dutch, German and Jewish surname, plural form of Linde. As a Dutch and West Flemish surname, from several placenames called Linden or Lienden.

lindsay.ety: From Lindsey in Lincolnshire, from Old English Lindesēġe, Lindesīġe (“Isle of Lind”), the Old English name of the city of Lincoln, Lincolnshire.

linnea.ety: A flower name coined in the eighteenth century, from, twinflower, named after the Swedish botanist Carl von Linné (1707-1778).

lisette.ety: From Elisabeth. The spelling of Elizabeth used in the Authorized Version of the New Testament.

lita.ety: A Dutch short form of names beginning with the element Liut-, from Old High German liut (“people”). Also associated with liten (“little”).

loic.ety: From Medieval Latin Ludovicus. Doublet of Louis.

lolita.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Lolita The name is from Spanish Lolita, diminutive of Lola, from the given name Dolores.

lori.ety: In some cases, a 20th century spelling variant of Laurie, from Laura. In other cases, a diminutive form of names such as Loretta and Lorraine.

lorraine.ety: Inherited from Middle English Loreyne, from Old French Loherraine, from loherenc (“Lotharingian”); compare Early Medieval Latin Lotharingia (ultimately named for Lothair II, who ruled it); compare Doublet of Lotharingia, German Lothringen.

lowell.ety: A Middle English diminutive of Old French lou + -el, meaning "little wolf". Akin to Wolfie.

luana.ety: Borrowed from English Luana. Made known in Hawaii by the play (1912) and film (1932) Bird of Paradise and later explained as Hawaiian luana (“leisure”).

lucette.ety: From a diminutive of the Latin name Lucia.

luci.ety: A modern nonstandard spelling of Lucy, from Lucia, from the Latin feminine form of the Latin praenomen Lucius, from lux "light".

lucinda.ety: Derived from Lucia with the suffix -inda, first used by Cervantes in Don Quixote (1605).

lucretia.ety: Originally from Latin lucrum (“gain, profit”). Many people with the given name have no doubt been named after others so named, not necessarily after the 6th-century-BC Roman noblewoman.

lula.ety: 19th-century variant of Lulu, nickname of Louisa and Lucy. In rare cases, shortened from Tallulah.

luther.ety: Borrowed from German Luther, from Old High German Liutheri (“male given name”), from Proto-West Germanic *Liudihari, composed of *liudi (“person, people”) and *hari (“army”).

lydia.ety: From Greek Λυδία (Lydía), from Ancient Greek Λυδία (“beauty, beautiful, noble one”).

lyndsey.ety: Spelling variant. A less common spelling of Lindsay or Lindsey.

macario.ety: Borrowed from Latin Macarius, from Ancient Greek Μακάριος.

macey.ety: As an English surname, variant of Massey. As a Slavic surname, Americanized from Slovak Macej, Carpathian Rusyn (Mačej), Polish Maciej, all variants of Matthew.

madalena.ety: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Madalena, after the town of Magdala, from Hebrew מגדל (migdál, “tower”).

maddy.ety: Short form of Madeleine or Short form of Madison + -y.

mads.ety: Borrowed from Danish Mads, a medieval Danish contraction of Mathias, historically also associated with Matthæus.

mael.ety: Borrowed from Breton Mael, from mael, literally “prince”.

maelle.ety: Borrowed from Breton Maelle, from maelle, literally “princess”.

magali.ety: Borrowed from Occitan Magalí Borrowed from Occitan Magalí.

mai.ety: Chinese surname with several origins: from Mandarin 麥 (“wheat”), from Mandarin and Cantonese 買 (“buy”) Cantonese form of 米 (see Mi). Romanized from 马 (see Ma) Romanized from 梅 (see Mei).

maiara.ety: From ma'e (“wealth, riches”) + îara (“lord, lady”), literally “the lady of riches”.

maila.ety: Originally a baby talk form of Maria; in some cases also from Amalia.

maisa.ety: A diminutive of names like Maria, Maija-Liisa, Marja-Liisa and Mailis.

maja.ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μαῖα.

malinda.ety: Variant of Melinda, used since the eighteenth century.

marcia.m: of pertaining to the gens Marcia, Marcian
marcia.ety: From Latin Marcia, feminine form of Marcius, a derivative of Marcus, ultimately from Mārs, the god of war.

marciano.m: of pertaining to Mārcus Mārcius, Marcian

marguerite.ety: Borrowed from French Marguerite in the 1860s. Doublet of Margaret, ultimately from the Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (“pearl”).

mari.ety: Short for Maria; also identical with Estonian mari (“berry”).

marian.ety: A variant of Marion, a medieval derivation of Mary, often also interpreted as a contraction of Mary and Ann, or as a variant of Mariana.

maribel.ety: Borrowed from Spanish Maribel, from a Blend of María + Isabel, from Spanish María Isabel. Maria + Isabel.

marit.ety: Contraction of Margareta (“Margaret”) first recorded in the 15th century.

marita.ety: Borrowed in the late 19th century from Norwegian Marita. By folk etymology, explained as a Spanish diminutive of Maria, by analogy with Anita.

maritza.ety: From Spanish Maritza, a diminutive of: María, from Marīa, from Μαρίᾱ, from מרים (miryām, “rebellion”); and Marta, from Martha, from Μάρθα, from מרתא (mārtā, “lady, mistress, ruler”), female counterpart of מרא (mārā, “lord, master, ruler”).

marsha.m: of pertaining to the gens Marcia, Marcian

marti.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Mārtīnus Latin Mārtīnus.

mateus.ety: From Old Galician-Portuguese Mateus, from Latin Matthaeus, from Ancient Greek Ματθαῖος, from Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ.

matthieu.ety: Inherited from Old French Mathieu, from Latin Matthaeus, from Ancient Greek Ματθαῖος, from Hebrew מַתִּתְיָהוּ (mattiṯyāhū), literally “gift of the Lord”.

matti.ety: Vernacular form of Matias and/or Matteus (both of the same origin), brought to Finland as Catholic saint's names. Already attested as a Finnish given name in medieval records.

mattis.ety: Patronymic surname from a pet form of the personal name Matthew.

mckayla.ety: Modern variant of Michaela, influenced by Mc-.

meabh.ety: From Middle Irish Medb, from Proto-Celtic *medwā, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu. Compare Middle Irish medb (“intoxicating”), from Proto-Celtic *medwos.

mehmet.ety: From Ottoman Turkish محمد (Mehmed, Mehmet), from Arabic مُحَمَّد. Doublet of Muhammad and Mahomet and Baphomet.

merle.ety: English 19th-century bird name from merle (“blackbird”), possibly also a variant of Muriel, Merrill, etc.

merlin.ety: From Middle English Merlyn, from Medieval Latin Merlinus and Old French Merlin, from Proto-Brythonic *Mor-ðin, literally “sea-hill”, from Proto-Celtic *mori (“sea”) + *dūnom (“stronghold, rampart”).

merry.m: ; forbearance to cause or allow harm to another.

meyer.ety: As a German and Alemannic German surname, from the noun Meier (“leaseholder of a manor”). Compare Maier, Mayer, Meier, Myer.

micael.ety: From Old Leonese Migael, from Latin Micaēl.

micha.ety: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָה (mīḵāh), whence also English Micah; see there for more information.

michel.ety: From Old French Michel, from Latin Michāēl,Michāēlem, borrowed from Koine Greek Μῐχᾱήλ, in turn borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mikha'él, “Michael”), literally “Who is like God?”.

mickael.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Michael See Michaël.

mika.ety: Ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָה (mīḵāh), shortened form of מִיכַיְהוּ (mīḵāyᵊhū, “who is like Yahweh”).

mikail.ety: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish میكائیل (mikail), from Arabic مِيكَائِيل, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל.

mikhail.ety: From Russian Михаи́л (“Michael”), from Hebrew מיכאל. Doublet of Michael.

miko.ety: From Mikko. Vernacular form of Mikael (“Michael”) attested since medieval times.

mildred.ety: From the name of an 8th-century English saint, Old English Mildþrȳþ.

milla.ety: From Latin Aemilia. Shortened from Estonian Emilie.

mio.ety: From the children's book Mio, min Mio by Astrid Lindgren. The book title is word play on Italian mio (“my”).

miro.ety: Probably from Slavic names like Proto-Slavic *Miroslavъ, Russian Влади́мир.

miron.ety: Transliteration of Міро́н. Borrowed from Ancient Greek Μύρων.

misha.ety: A transliteration of the Russian Ми́ша, a hypocoristic for Михаи́л, the Russian equivalent of Michael, from Hebrew מיכאל.

misty.ety: From the adjective misty, but sometimes also (like Missy) used as a nickname for Melissa.

modesto.ety: Inherited from Latin Modestus From Latin Modestus.

moise.ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Mōysēs Latin Mōysēs.

mona.ety: Anglicized from Irish and Scottish Gaelic Muadhnait, from Middle Irish múad (“noble”).

monika.ety: From Latin Monica, name of the mother of St. Augustine, of uncertain origin and meaning; suggestions include Ancient Greek μόνος (“alone”) and Latin moneō (“to advise”), but likely of Punic origin.

montana.ety: Borrowed from Spanish montaña From Latin montāna the US state via Spanish montaña (“mountain”) the surname from Spanish Montaña topographic surname.

morgana.ety: From Old Welsh or Old Breton Morgen, literally “sea-born”.

moussa.ety: Borrowed from Arabic مُوسَى (“Moses”). Doublet of Moïse.

muriel.ety: Anglicized form of Scottish Gaelic Muireall, from muir (“sea”), from Old Irish muir, from Proto-Celtic *mori, from Proto-Indo-European *móri; + geal (“white, bright”), from Old Irish gel, from Proto-Celtic *gelos (“yellow.

murray.ety: Scottish surname derived from the place name Moray in northeastern Scotland, from Medieval Latin Moravia, Morauia, from Scottish Gaelic Moireibh, Moireabh, Moreb, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *mori (“sea”) + *trebā (“settlement”).

nabila.ety: Borrowed from Arabic نَبِيلَة, feminine of نَبِيل (“noble”).

naima.ety: Variant of Naimi, from Naemi, the equivalent of English Naomi in older versions of the Finnish Bible.

nana.ety: Not certain whether directly derived from Armenian Նանե, or by association with the ancient Iranian goddess of the same name.

napoleon.ety: From French Napoléon, from Italian Napoleone, name of an early saint, of uncertain origin; possibly from the Germanic clan name Nibelung.

nassim.ety: Borrowed from Arabic نسيم or Persian نسیم.

nataliya.ety: Transliteration of Ната́лья. Ultimately from Latin Natalia.

natalya.ety: Transliteration of Russian Ната́лья. Doublet of Natalie.

ned.ety: From rebracketing of the phrase mine Ed to my Ned.

neela.ety: Through spelling pronunciation from English Neela, from Sanskrit नील.

nelle.ety: From Ellen spelled backwards. Popularized by author Harper Lee, whose first name Nelle was so derived from her grandmother’s.

nels.ety: Anglicization of Norwegian Nils and Swedish Nils, reflecting the pronunciation of the name among Scandinavian immigrants to North America, or matched to Nelson.

nettie.ety: Suffixed with -ie, compare Neddie and Nellie, respectively from Edward and Eleanor.

neville.ety: A Norman baronial surname, de Neville, from place names in Normandy, Néville, from Old French Neville, literally “Néel's estate” or Neuville, literally “new settlement”, equivalent to nuef + ville.

nevin.ety: A rare Anglicization of Irish Naomhán, a diminutive of naomh (“saint”).

newton.ety: Inherited from Middle English Neweton, from Old English nēowa tūn (“new town”). Compare same construction in Italian Napoli (“Naples”) and in Arabic نَابُلُس (“Nablus”).

nicolette.ety: From Nicole. Feminine form of Nicolas (“Nicholas”).

niels.ety: Medieval contraction of Latin Nicolaus, Nicholaus, from the Ancient Greek Νικόλαος. Cognate with English Nicholas.

nigel.ety: English form of Latin Nigellus, from nigellus (“slightly black”), diminutive of niger (“black”), used in the Middle Ages to Latinize Norman Néel and Old Irish Níall, from which the former is derived via Old Norse Njáll.

nikita.ety: From the Russian Ники́та, a male given name, from Ancient Greek Νικήτας (“conqueror”) also a male given name (and name of various saints). The Greek word derives from νῑ́κη (“victory”).

niklas.ety: Vernacular form of Nikolas, Nikolaus, probably fairly recently borrowed from Swedish Niklas.

nikole.ety: Borrowed from the French Nicole, from Ancient Greek Νικόλαος (Nikólaos), from νίκη (níkē, “victory”) + λαός (laós, “people”).

nils.ety: Borrowed from Swedish Nils. A variant of the more common Danish Niels.

noam.ety: From Hebrew נועם (“pleasantness; a male name”).

nona.ety: Feminine form of the Roman gens name Nōnus, from nōnus (“the ninth”).

norris.m: a northerner, a migrant from the north
norris.ety: An Anglo-Norman surname, from Old French norreis (“a northerner, a migrant from the north”). More at French norois.

novella.ety: From novella, feminine form of novello (“new, early”).

nuria.m: The Mother of God of Núria
nuria.ety: From the Roman Catholic Catalan epithet of the Virgin Mary La Mare de Déu de Núria (“The Mother of God of Núria”), from the place name Núria (Vall de Núria, “Núria valley”).

oceane.ety: Modern feminine form of Océan, from Latin Ōceanus, Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός, the god of sea and the name of an early Christian saint.

octavian.ety: From Latin Octavianus, from Octāvius + -ianus (“-ian: forming adjectives”), initially used to distinguish the future Roman emperor upon his adoption by his uncle Gaius Julius Caesar.

octavius.ety: From Latin Octāvius (“Roman praenomen and nomen”), from octavius (“eighth”), probably initially in reference the child's birth order or the month of their birth in the Roman calendar.

odie.ety: Separate origins as diminutives of British name Odell and Germanic name Odin; later used as nickname for additional given names.

oisin.ety: From oisín (“fawn”), from os (“deer”) + -ín; name of a hero in Irish mythology.

oksana.ety: Transliteration of Окса́на. A form of the name Ксе́ния, from Ancient Greek ξενία (“hospitality”).

olaya.ety: From Latin Eulalia, from Ancient Greek Εὐλαλία, from εὔλαλος (“sweetly speaking”). Cognate with Spanish Eulalia, Galician Olalla and French Eulalie.

oleg.ety: Borrowed from Russian Оле́г, a Varangian name, ultimately from Old Norse Helgi (“holy, sacred or blessed”). Cognate to modern Scandinavian Helge.

ora.ety: First appeared in the 19th century when similar sounding names like Cora, Dora and Nora were in fashion.

ostap.ety: Transliteration of Ukrainian Оста́п, ultimately from Ancient Greek Εὐστάθιος. Doublet of Eustace.

oswald.ety: Inherited from Old English Ōsweald, from ōs (“god, deity”) + weald (“power”). Cognate with German Answald, Ásvaldur, and Norwegian Nynorsk Åsvald.

otilia.ety: From Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda.

pamela.ety: Invented by Sir Philip Sidney for his pastoral poem The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia (c 1593).

pascal.m: Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter
pascal.ety: From Latin Paschālis, from paschālis (“Paschal; of or pertaining to Easter”), from pascha (“Easter”) + -ālis, for birth on Easter, or in honor of the 9th-century pope Paschal I (died 824).

pasha.ety: From Armenian Փաշա (Pʻaša), from Middle Armenian փաշայ (“pasha”).

patsy.ety: From the Short form of Patricia or Patrick + -sy.

pauline.ety: From French Pauline, in turn from Latin Paulīna; in regular use since the 19th century.

percival.ety: From Old French Perceval, name of a knight in a twelfth century Arthurian romance by the French poet Chrétien de Troyes.

perpetua.ety: Borrowed from Latin Perpetua, name of an early saint, from perpetuus (“continuous, perpetual”).

perrin.ety: From a Middle English pet-form of Peter, from an Old French diminutive of Pierre.

peterson.ety: English, Scottish, and German surname, from Peter + -son.

phil.ety: Shortened from Philip, from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος, which see for more information.

philippa.ety: Feminine form of Philippus from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος, literally “Lover of Horses”.

philomena.ety: From Latin Philomēna, from Ancient Greek Φιλουμένη, literally “beloved”. Name of an alleged early martyr whose remains were discovered in 1802 in Rome.

phineas.ety: From Ancient Greek Φινέας, alternative form of Φινεύς. Alternative source from Hebrew (פִינְחָס).

pia.ety: From Latin Pia, feminine form of the papal name Pius, from pius (“pious”).

polly.ety: Nickname for Mary, created by rhyming with Molly.

portia.ety: From Latin Porcia, a feminine form of the gens name Porcius (the gens of the Cato the Elder and his famous descendants), from porcus (“pig”).

primrose.ety: The surname derives from a place name in Fife, Scotland; Watson (1926) derived this from Pictish/Proto-Brythonic *prenn (“wood, tree”) + *rros (“moor, heath”).

prisca.ety: Latin feminine form of the cognomen Prīscus, from prīscus (“former, ancient, old-fashioned”).

queenie.m: The wife, consort, or widow of a king.

rachelle.ety: 20th-century variant of Rachel, from French Rachelle, or possibly coined independently of it.

raffi.ety: From Armenian Րաֆֆի (Raffi), from Arabic رَفِيع (“lofty”).

rainer.ety: Variant of Rayner, a patronymic surname from a medieval given name from Proto-Germanic *raginą (“counsel by the gods”) + *harjaz (“army”). Also borrowed from modern German.

rainey.ety: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Raighne (“descendant of Raighne”), a Gaelicized form of the Old Norse personal name Rognvaldr.

raisa.m: easy; easy to understand, easy to do

raleigh.ety: From Old English rā, rāha (“roe deer”) + lēah (“woodland, clearing”). Equivalent to roe + -ley (“lea”).

rami.ety: Borrowed from Arabic رَامِي, masculine singular construct form of رَامٍ (rāmin). This surname is predominantly found in Morocco and India.

ramsey.ety: From Old English hramsa (“wild garlic”) + īeġ (“island”).

rana.m: a title of various Indian, Bangladeshi and Nepalese kings
rana.ety: From Bengali রাণা (rana), a noun meaning “a title of various Indian, Bangladeshi and Nepalese kings”, from Magadhi Prakrit.

rand.ety: From Afrikaans rand, from English rand; compare English rand.

randi.ety: Contraction of Ragnfrid, from Old Norse Ragnfríðr, from ragn (“advice, judgment”) + fríðr (“beautiful”).

rashed.ety: From Bengali রাশেদ (raśed), from Arabic رَاشِد (“mature, well guided”).

rasmus.ety: From the Latin saints' name Erasmus, from Ancient Greek Erasmos "beloved". Used in Denmark since the fifteenth century.

reilly.ety: From Irish Ó Raghallaigh, a surname meaning "descendants of Raghallach".

reine.ety: A more gallicized form of Régine, from Latin Regina (“queen”).

rhonda.ety: Modern coinage explained as Welsh rhon (“pike, lance”) + da (“good”).

richmond.ety: From Middle English Rychemund, from a name cognate to French Richemont (“town in Normandy”). Equivalent to rich + mound.

ricki.ety: As a female name also from Erica.

ridley.ety: Place names in England, Old English hrēad (“reeds”) or rydde (“cleared land”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Thus, equivalent to reed or rid + -ley (“lea”).

rina.ety: Short form of names ending in -rina, such as Katrina, Marina and Larina. Also borrowed from other European languages, such as Italian, in the 20th century.

ripley.ety: From the Old English folk name for the Anglian tribe, *Hrype + Old English lēah (“woodland clearing”).

rochelle.ety: Habitational or topographic name from places in France, La Rochelle, from Old French rochelle diminutive form of roche (“rock”).

rocio.ety: From rocío (“dew”), shortened from María (del) Rocío, an epithet of the Virgin Mary in Almonte, Spain.

rock.ety: As an English surname, from the noun rock. Also as an English surname, misdivision of Middle English atter oke (“at the oak”).

rommel.ety: From the Dutch surname, from rommelen (“to rumble”). Also a spelling variant of Rummel.

ronaldo.ety: Borrowed from English Ronald Borrowed from English Ronald, anglicized from a Scottish Gaelic form of Old Norse Rǫgnvaldr, from rǫgn (“advice”) + valdr (“power”), later partly merged with the Continental Germanic equivalent Reynold.

roni.ety: 20th century rendering of English Ronnie. It can also be explained as a short form of the Latin (ultimately Ancient Greek) saint's name Hieronymus and of biblical Aaron.

ronny.ety: Shortening of Ronald + -y. A less common spelling of Ronnie.

roosevelt.m: wild rose / poppy? + open country; field
roosevelt.ety: From a Dutch name of a farm, either Rozenveld (one in Zeeland) or Ruiseveld (one in Brabant), from Middle Dutch; the former could be a compound of rose (“wild rose / poppy?”) + velt (“open country.

rosaleen.ety: Anglicized from Irish Róisín, a diminutive of Rose.

rosalind.ety: From Proto-Germanic *hrussą (“horse”) and *linþaz (“soft; weak, tender”), associated by medieval folk etymology with Spanish rosa linda "lovely rose".

rosaline.ety: An elaborate form of Rosalie, or a simplified form of Rosalind.

roscoe.ety: From a place in Lancashire, from Old Norse rá (“roebuck”) + skógr (“forest”).

rosendo.ety: Surname from transferred use of given name, of Spanish, Galician, or Portuguese origin, from Medieval Latin Rudesindus, from the Germanic (Gothic) name Rudesind, composed of the elements *𐌷𐍂𐍉𐌸𐍃 (“glory.

rosina.ety: An Italian pet form of Rosa borrowed in the nineteenth century, particularly from the character in Rossini's opera The Barber of Seville (1816).

rune.ety: From Old Norse Rúni, from rúni (“good friend”). Also a short form of compound names with the element run (such as Runolv).

rupert.ety: A German name, brought to England by Prince Rupert of the Rhine in the seventeenth century. Doublet of Robert.

rush.ety: As an English surname, from the noun rush (“waterside plant, plant in marshes”). Also as an English surname, from the archaic noun rush (“beehive”), from French ruche.

sabine.ety: From the Latin saint's name Sabina.

sabra.ety: Borrowed from Hebrew צַבָּר (tsabár, “prickly pear cactus”), from Arabic صَبَّار (“cactus”).

sadiya.ety: From Bengali সাদিয়া (śadiẏa), from Arabic سَعْدِيَّة (“fortunate, happy”).

safira.ety: Borrowed from Italian Saffira, from Ancient Greek Σαπφειρη, likely from σάπφειρος.

saida.ety: From Kazakh Саида (Saıyda), from Arabic سَيِّد (“master, sir, generous”).

sajid.ety: From Bengali সাজিদ (śajid), from Arabic سَاجِد (“prostrated”).

salah.ety: As an Islamic/Arabic surname, as well as a Jewish adoption of it, from صَلاة (“prayer”) or صَلاح (“righteousness”).

sallie.ety: A less common spelling of Sally; see -ie.

sander.ety: Short form of Aleksander, also used as a short form of Alexander (“male given name”).

sanders.ety: From the Middle English Sander, a shortened form of Alexander + suffix -s.

sanya.ety: Variant of Saniyah, Saniyya, from Arabic سنيّة (“radiant”).

sascha.ety: Russian Саша, a pet form of Александра ( =Alexandra), cognate to Sasha.

saxon.ety: Partially from Middle English Saxe, Sax; from Old English *Seaxa (attested in plural Seaxan), from Proto-West Germanic *Sahsan, plural of Proto-West Germanic *Sahsō.

schuyler.ety: A Dutch surname (cf. scholier) from German Schüler (“scholar, student”); brought to America by seventeenth-century Dutch immigrants. Doublet of scholar and schooler.

selim.ety: From Swedish Selim, from Arabic سليم; partly also from forms of Anselmi.

selina.ety: From Selene. From the Ancient Greek Σελήνη, from σέλας (“light”).

selma.ety: Taken to use in the 19th century when similar-sounding names, Elma, Thelma, Alma, Wilma, etc. were in vogue.

september.ety: From Middle English, from late Old English, from Old French septembre, Latin September (“seventh month”), from septem (“seven”), which see; September was the seventh month in the Roman calendar.

seymour.ety: From a Norman surname from a place in Normandy, from Old French Saint-Maur, from Late Latin Sanctus Maurus (“Saint Maurus”). The name is cognate to Murry and Maurice.

shana.ety: Anglicized variant of the Welsh name Siân (pet form Siana) - or a version of the French name Jeanne.

shaquille.ety: A fanciful spelling of Arabic شَكِيل (“handsome”).
